title: How much time do you guys spend on things players might never notice?
author: old-murmel
selftext: I have been spending to many hours on the night sky in my semi low poly game, designing, playing then adjusting and so on to get the right look, not to realistic but also not too cartoony. Do you think players even notice? And how much time do you guys put into all the small details? (and how do you like it?)

comments.author: StellarSoupStudio
comments.body: Oh tons, that's the polish

replies.author: Such--Balance
replies.body: What does Poland have to do with this?!?!

comments.author: Fincut
comments.body:
Way too much, and I’d do it again. I made this game mostly for my wife and me, so nobody was telling me to stop.

Mine is the sinking of the ships. It’s a ship game, so you see it all the time, and I couldn’t leave it alone. When a ship goes under, the water actually behaves like water: it swallows red light first, then green, so the wreck turns blue green and then dark the deeper it sinks. The surface bends the light too, so the hull looks shallower and wobbles with every wave. Underneath there are explosions, and the bubbles rising up are full of smoke.

Do players notice? Probably not consciously. But I know it’s there, and I still enjoy watching a ship go down after hundreds of hours.

If anyone wants to see it, there’s a free browser demo, sorry for the plug: [https://wildstone-studios.com/?k=aigamedev3](https://wildstone-studios.com/?k=aigamedev3)

comments.author: Shleepy1
comments.body: I think it depends on the gameplay. Hectic games don’t usually allow to take in the scenery that much, but in my experience, many gamers look for details if the game gives the time or rewards it

comments.author: johnesco
comments.body: The white lines on the road of my game didn't need to be any smoother, but found it was a no-cost (to framerate) to make it look so much better (to me) but not sure if a player would notice.

replies.author: Such--Balance
replies.body:
Actually not noticing IS the win in a lot of those cases.

People play a game. And the lines they see on the road just look..a bit off. They are just not quite right. A small annoyance that keeps bubbling up every time those weird lines are encountered.

Polish your game, and less slight annoyances will pop up in the player.

comments.author: Original-League-6094
comments.body: Polish is something players notice without noticing, if that makes sense. Most people can't articulate why they like a specific game's art over another, and most people can't point out any tiny details in anything...and yet stuff that is well polished and has a lot of thought into it resonates with them nonetheless.

comments.author: IndianaNetworkAdmin
comments.body:
My game started with a day/night system.

Then I decided I wanted dynamic clouds. So the clouds change depending on weather.

Then I decided I wanted predictable seed-based weather. So I set a static seed and have a date system in place with weather.

Then I realized the fog would change depending on the weather. So I added humidity calculation, season, and fog dynamics. Fog rises from the lowest valleys, thick in the morning, then burns off over the course of the day.

Then I realized that the color hues in the sky would change depending on the season and weather.

I've been working on the weather and time components for two years now.

The problem is that all the ground assets look like hot garbage now, so I need to clean up all the shaders.

It started with [https://github.com/eisclimber/DynamicDayNightCycles](https://github.com/eisclimber/DynamicDayNightCycles) and snowballed from there.

What it cant do is be distracting to the experince of the game, The theme of the game has to be consiestent or the player will notice.
